Freemium vs. Free Trial: What Should Stay Free?

A decision at a Bengaluru analytics company shows why "make it free" is not one idea but two, and why choosing the wrong one can quietly bankrupt a product that looks like it is growing.

A Tuesday morning in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of June 2024, Meera Iyer, vice-president of growth at Saksham Analytics, opened the pre-read for Friday's board meeting and found a single slide circled in red by her CEO. Saksham built a no-code analytics layer that let finance and operations teams in mid-market companies connect to their transaction systems and build dashboards without writing SQL. The company had signed roughly four hundred paying customers since its 2021 founding, priced at an average of ₹42,000 a year per account, and had raised its Series A on the strength of a clean, sales-light growth motion: a fourteen-day free trial, full product access, a sales call offered around day seven, and a card required only if the prospect wanted to keep going past day fourteen. It had worked. It had also stopped working. Monthly trial signups had held flat at about 2,400 for two straight quarters despite a 30% increase in performance-marketing spend, and the blended cost of acquiring a paying customer had crept up to ₹18,500. The board's question, stated plainly in the red circle, was whether Saksham should scrap the trial and open a permanently free tier instead — the way a fast-growing rival had done four months earlier, doubling its signup volume within a quarter, at least according to the LinkedIn posts its founder kept sharing.

Meera's problem was that she had, until that morning, treated "free trial" and "freemium" as roughly interchangeable marketing words for "the thing before the paywall." They are not. They are two different architectures for who gets to use the product for nothing, for how long, and at whose ongoing expense — and the choice between them would determine not just Saksham's signup curve but its cloud bill, its support headcount, and whether its sales team could still tell a credible story about who a "real" prospect was. She had until Friday to bring the board a recommendation grounded in numbers rather than in what a competitor's founder chose to post.

The idea, defined precisely

A free trial is time-boxed or usage-boxed access to a product that a person cannot keep once the box is used up unless they pay. The defining feature is an expiry: the free period is an event with a start and an end, engineered to force a decision. A freemium model is different in kind, not just degree: it is a permanently free version of the product — a specific, deliberately bounded slice of the full offering — that a user may keep using forever, with no clock running and no card ever required, alongside a paid version that unlocks more. The free tier under freemium is not an appetiser before a meal that must eventually be paid for; it is a standing asset the company chooses to fund indefinitely, in the hope that a minority of the people using it will eventually need more than it gives them.

The economics behind this distinction are recent. Time-boxed software evaluation is as old as shareware — WordPerfect and early antivirus tools shipped 30-day trial diskettes in the 1980s because duplicating a diskette had a real marginal cost that made "free forever" unthinkable. Freemium became viable only once software delivery moved to the cloud and the marginal cost of serving one more inactive or lightly active user fell close to zero. The term itself is usually credited to Jarid Lukin, a manager at the alternative-content firm Alacra, who used it in a 2006 internal document, and to the venture investor Fred Wilson, who popularised it the same year in a blog post describing the business model behind Skype and Flickr. What Wilson was naming was not a marketing trick but a distribution strategy: give away a permanently useful core product to as many people as will take it, and let a small, predictable percentage fund the rest through upgrades.

The sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: a free trial turns the sales pitch itself into the product, but only for as long as the clock runs; freemium turns a slice of the product into its own permanent acquisition channel, at the cost of paying to keep that slice running forever. Everything that follows in a pricing discussion is really an argument about which of those two economics — a burst cost that resolves quickly, or a standing cost that persists — a given business can actually afford.

How the choice actually gets made, mechanically

Practitioners who have done this well do not start by asking "should we go freemium." They start by drawing the line inside the product — the boundary between what a non-paying user gets forever and what a paying user gets additionally — and they draw it through a sequence of decisions that is usually left implicit in casual conversation about pricing.

The first decision is the gating mechanism: will the free line be drawn by feature (certain capabilities simply do not exist below the paywall), by usage (every capability exists, but a quota caps how much of it can be consumed), or by time (everything exists, but only until a clock runs out)? These are not interchangeable; they produce different user psychology, discussed further below. The second decision is where inside that mechanism to set the actual line — which features, or what quota, or how many days — and this has to be set with reference to two separate things: how much of the product's real value a user must experience before the free version stops being persuasive, and how much it costs Saksham, in cloud compute, storage and support minutes, to let someone sit on that line indefinitely. The third decision is the trigger point: the specific moment, inside the product, where a free user hits the line and is shown an upgrade path — a warning at 90% of a data-retention quota, a locked "Export to Excel" button, a "your 14th day starts tomorrow" banner. The fourth, frequently skipped, decision is instrumentation: building the analytics to see, cohort by cohort, where free users get real value, where they get stuck, and where they simply leave, because without that data the first three decisions are guesses that never get corrected. The fifth is deciding what non-paying users are owed in support — community forum only, or a real queue — because that line, too, has a cost. The sixth is reconciling the free tier with the sales motion: freemium tends to pair with pure self-serve upgrade, while a free trial often carries a sales rep alongside it, because the trial's expiry date is itself a natural excuse for a call.

Saksham's existing free trial already encoded several of these choices without anyone having named them: the gating mechanism was pure time (14 days, full feature set), the trigger was a scheduled sales call on day seven, and support during the trial ran through the same queue as paying customers. A freemium alternative would require Meera to make four decisions Saksham had never had to make before: which features stay locked forever (she proposed capping the free tier at three dashboards, thirty days of data retention rather than the paid tier's unlimited, and no single sign-on or data export); how a free account is nudged toward upgrading (an in-product meter showing "2 of 3 dashboards used"); what support a free user receives (community documentation only); and, critically, what happens to the cost of serving a free account that never expires.

A worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Meera built her recommendation around one spreadsheet, and it is worth walking through it the way she did, because the numbers are what changed her board's mind, not the concept.

Under the existing free-trial model, roughly 12,000 visitors reached Saksham's signup page each month, of whom 2,400 (20%) started a trial. Of those, 19% converted to a paid plan within the fourteen-day window — a rate Saksham tracked closely because the trial resolves itself quickly and cleanly. That is 456 new paying customers a month. At an average revenue per account of ₹42,000 a year, or ₹3,500 a month, that cohort added ₹15,96,000 in new monthly recurring revenue every month it repeated. The cost of serving a trial user was small and temporary: cloud compute and storage for a fourteen-day sandbox ran to about ₹80 per trial user, or ₹1,92,000 across the full monthly cohort — a cost that vanished from the books two weeks after it was incurred, because trial accounts that did not convert were deleted.

Meera then modelled a freemium alternative using assumptions she deliberately kept conservative. Removing the card requirement and the expiry date, she assumed, would roughly triple monthly signups to 7,200, since much of the friction in the current funnel came from prospects unwilling to start a clock they might forget about. But a freemium account carries no forcing event, so she assumed a much lower resolution rate: each month, about 8% of the active free base would either convert to a paid plan or churn out entirely (delete the account or go inactive), and of that 8%, one in eight — 1% of the active base — would be a conversion rather than a departure. Running that ratio to a steady state, several months after launch, gives an active free-user base of 7,200 ÷ 0.08 = 90,000 accounts sitting on the books at any given time. Of those, 1% convert every month: 900 new paying customers monthly, very nearly double the 456 the trial produced. New monthly recurring revenue from that cohort: 900 × ₹3,500 = ₹31,50,000 — roughly double the trial figure as well.

Read across that last row and the appeal of freemium starts to look different. The trial's cost to serve is a small, self-liquidating expense that disappears within two weeks. Freemium's cost to serve — ₹95 a month per free account, mostly cloud compute and storage for dashboards that free users keep open and refreshing indefinitely, multiplied by an accumulated base of 90,000 — is a permanent monthly drain of ₹85.5 lakh that does not disappear until an account converts or is deleted. Freemium roughly doubled Saksham's rate of new-customer creation, but it did so by taking on a standing liability more than fifty times larger than the one it replaced. The revenue gain compounds every month a customer stays subscribed (Saksham's average tenure ran close to thirty months); the cost is a flat recurring number that only shrinks if the free base itself shrinks. Whether freemium is a good trade for Saksham therefore depends entirely on how fast that ₹95-a-month figure can be pushed down, and on how confident Meera could be that it would not go up.

That second question turned out to matter more than the first. Saksham's product team was, in the same quarter, building an AI-generated "insights" feature that would call a large language model to summarise a dashboard in plain English — a feature product wanted to offer even to free users, as a hook. Each such call carried a real inference cost. Meera reran the model assuming the free tier included fifty AI-generated insights a month per account, at an estimated ₹1.90 per call: that alone would add ₹95 a month per free account, doubling the fully loaded cost to serve to ₹190, and lifting the steady-state monthly bill for the free base to ₹1.71 crore — a number that would erase most of the gross margin the freemium tier was supposed to be building toward. This second pass was the one that reached the board packet: it showed that the freemium decision was not really a growth decision at all, but a decision about how much of an unpriced, LLM-metered feature Saksham could responsibly give away before the free tier stopped being an asset and became a liability that happened to also generate some new customers.

The nuances a learner has to sit with

Freemium is not a cheap tier — it is a different kind of relationship

The single most common confusion is treating "freemium" as a synonym for "our lowest-priced plan is free." A discounted entry-level paid plan still asks for a card and still assumes the buyer intends, eventually, to pay something. A true freemium tier makes no such assumption: the large majority of people on it are expected to remain there forever, and the product has to be designed, and costed, on that basis. If a team cannot say out loud that 95% or more of free users will never pay, it has probably built a confusing extra pricing tier rather than a freemium acquisition engine.

The free line has to be drawn against cost-to-serve, not just against feature completeness

It is tempting to set the free tier by asking "what is the smallest set of features that still feels useful?" That question ignores the other half of the equation: some features that feel small to a user are expensive to keep running forever — AI calls, large file storage, real-time data syncing — while others that feel generous to a user cost the vendor almost nothing at cloud scale. The free line should sit at the intersection of "still genuinely useful" and "cheap enough to fund for an unbounded population," which is exactly why Saksham's AI-insights feature, not its dashboard count, turned out to be the binding constraint.

Feature-gating, usage-gating and time-gating produce different user psychology

A feature-gated wall declares scarcity from the first session — the user knows immediately what they are not getting — which is honest but can suppress initial adoption. A usage-gated wall lets a user feel unrestricted right up until the ceiling, producing a sharper, more motivated upgrade moment precisely because the user has already built a habit before hitting the limit. A time-gated wall is the bluntest instrument: it forces a decision regardless of how much value has actually been realised, which is why trial conversion rates are so sensitive to when, inside the fourteen days, real value first appears.

Freemium works where value compounds without the vendor's ongoing involvement

Products that rely on network effects, sharing, or simple habitual utility — a messaging app, a design tool, a note-taking app — can sustain a large free population because each free user adds some value to the network (referrals, shared documents, brand exposure) even while consuming resources. Products that require consultative selling, custom implementation, or deep account management do not get this benefit: a free user of an enterprise resource-planning system generates no referral value proportional to the cost of supporting them, which is why freemium is rare in that category regardless of how it performs in consumer software.

Freemium tells you about activation and habit, not about willingness to pay for anything you have not yet built

A large, engaged free user base is genuine evidence that people find a specific, narrow slice of the product valuable enough to keep using. It is not evidence that those same people would pay for some future premium feature, nor is it a substitute for a pricing study. Teams sometimes point to freemium adoption numbers as proof a price increase or new tier will be accepted; the free base was never asked that question and its behaviour does not answer it.

Freemium is routinely confused with a loss leader

A loss leader — a retailer selling milk below cost to bring shoppers into the store — assumes the same buyer eventually pays full price for something else in that same visit. Freemium's economics are different: most of the free cohort will never pay for anything, ever, and the free tier's return comes instead from the minority who convert, from word-of-mouth and brand distribution the free users generate, or, for a two-sided marketplace, from the other side of the market the free side helps attract. Modelling freemium as a loss leader — expecting the free spend to be recouped from the same user — leads to disappointment when it is not.

Cannibalisation is the risk nobody checks before launch

If a free tier is set too generously relative to the cheapest paid plan, existing paying customers will notice they qualify for the free tier and downgrade. The cheapest pre-launch diagnostic is embarrassingly simple and almost never run: take the usage histogram of your current lowest-paying customer segment and check what fraction of them would fit comfortably inside the proposed free limits. If the answer is more than a few percent, the free tier is not additive — it is a discount that some existing customers will discover.

Support cost is a hidden, regressive tax on the free tier

Free users file support tickets at rates that are often similar to paying users in absolute terms but generate zero revenue to offset the cost, meaning the effective cost-to-serve of a support-eligible free tier can be dramatically higher than the compute bill alone suggests. Any freemium plan needs an explicit, stated decision about what a non-paying user is owed — community forum, chatbot, or a real human queue — made before launch, not discovered afterward in a headcount request.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

The same two architectures play out differently depending on who is on the other end of the free account, and on how much runway the company funding it has left.

In consumer software, freemium is close to the default because acquisition cost per user is near zero, scale is enormous, and a free tier can often be monetised a second way — through advertising, or through the free user's role in a network — even before any subscription conversion occurs; Spotify and Duolingo both run this model at scale, with tens of millions of permanently non-paying users whose scale itself is part of the pitch to advertisers and to future paying converts. In B2B software sold through a self-serve, product-led motion — developer tools, analytics layers like Saksham's, lightweight collaboration software — freemium is increasingly common because the buyer and the user are the same person and the sale does not require a human, so a well-designed free tier can do real qualification work. In B2B software sold top-down to large enterprise buyers, freemium is rare and often actively wrong: a hypothetical enterprise resource-planning vendor selling to large industrial distributors, call it Samagra CRM, would gain almost nothing from a free tier, because its buyers are procurement committees who need a guided evaluation, a security review and an implementation plan, not a self-serve trial — a time-boxed sandbox with a named sales contact serves that motion far better than an open, unmonitored free account ever could. In marketplaces, "free" typically subsidises only one side: a marketplace commonly lets sellers list for free to build supply liquidity, and recovers its economics through a take rate charged to buyers or through paid promotion for sellers who want visibility, which means the free tier's purpose is not lead generation at all but market-making.

Company stage matters just as much as category. An early-stage, cash-constrained company usually cannot afford the standing liability a large free base represents — every free account is a monthly draw on a runway that is already short — which is why most seed- and Series A-stage SaaS businesses, Saksham included until 2024, default to a trial: its cost resolves itself within weeks rather than compounding for years. Freemium becomes affordable once a company has either driven the marginal cost of serving a free user down through infrastructure scale and negotiated cloud pricing, or has raised enough capital to treat the free base explicitly as a strategic distribution investment rather than an operating expense. This is why freemium tends to appear, or to be affordable at real scale, later in a company's life than a free trial does, even though a freemium *idea* is often the one an early-stage founder finds most appealing on a whiteboard.

Common mistakes, and how to catch them cheaply

Mistake 1 — mistaking signups for growth

The symptom is a team celebrating a freemium launch because signups tripled, while paid conversion and revenue stay essentially flat for two or three quarters afterward. The underlying misunderstanding is treating volume itself as the objective, when volume only matters if the free tier creates a genuine moment where a real constraint is felt. The cheapest diagnostic is to trace the cohort from signup through to the specific in-product event meant to trigger upgrade interest — if a negligible share of free users ever reach that event, the funnel has more people in it but no more pressure pushing them through it.

Mistake 2 — shipping a free tier with no cost ceiling

The symptom is a cloud or inference bill that grows unpredictably and disconnectedly from revenue, discovered by finance rather than by product. The underlying misunderstanding is designing the free tier around what feels generous to a user without ever pricing what that generosity costs at scale, especially for any feature that calls a metered external service such as an LLM. The cheapest diagnostic, run before launch and revisited monthly, is a single number: fully loaded cost to serve per free account, tracked against the trend of paid gross margin per account, exactly as Meera did with Saksham's AI-insights feature before it shipped rather than after.

Mistake 3 — bolting freemium onto a sales-led motion

The symptom is a sales team complaining that free signups never respond to outreach, while enterprise deal cycles that used to close smoothly start stalling. The underlying misunderstanding is applying a self-serve tactic to a buyer who actually needs, and expects, a guided evaluation — the free tier signals "this is a self-serve tool," which undercuts the credibility of a subsequent six-figure enterprise pitch. The cheapest diagnostic is to check, for every enterprise deal closed in the last two quarters, whether it originated from the free tier or from a targeted, sales-initiated trial; if the answer is overwhelmingly the latter, the free tier is not doing the qualification work it was meant to do for that segment.

Mistake 4 — a free tier generous enough to cannibalise existing customers

The symptom is a wave of downgrade requests from paying customers shortly after a freemium launch, often customers who quietly explain that the new free plan "covers what we actually use." The underlying misunderstanding is setting free-tier limits by looking only at prospective new users, never at the usage patterns of the company's own existing lowest-tier customers. The cheapest diagnostic, described above and worth repeating because so few teams run it, is a simple histogram check of current paid usage against the proposed free limits before the free tier ever ships.

What good looks like

The clearest publicly visible example of this decision made well is Canva's early free tier, built around a large library of templates and a genuinely complete design canvas available to anyone with no card and no expiry, gated instead on a narrower set of premium stock photography, brand-kit features for teams, and background-removal tools. The choice mattered because Canva's marginal cost of serving a free designer — mostly bandwidth for lightweight image assets — stayed low even as its free base grew into the tens of millions, while the features it reserved for paying customers were disproportionately the ones that mattered to teams and businesses rather than individual hobbyists, which meant the free tier converted through organic team growth rather than through an artificial wall. Zoom's early growth shows the complementary lesson from the time-gating side: rather than choosing purely between freemium and trial, it blended the two, offering unlimited one-to-one calls for free forever but capping group meetings at forty minutes — a usage-and-time hybrid that let millions use the product habitually at near-zero marginal cost to Zoom, while placing the one limitation, meeting length, exactly at the point where a real business need (an hour-long team meeting) created a natural, low-friction reason to pay. In both cases, the company that got this right did not ask "freemium or trial" as an abstract preference; it asked what a permanently free user would cost to serve, and placed the free line exactly where that cost stayed low while the value delivered stayed real.

What Meera decided, and what to sit with

Meera's recommendation to the board, delivered that Friday, was neither a wholesale switch to freemium nor a defence of the status quo. She proposed keeping the fourteen-day, sales-assisted trial for Saksham's enterprise segment — accounts above two hundred employees, where a guided evaluation and a named sales contact were, the deal data showed, doing real qualification work — while launching a genuine freemium tier for self-serve small teams: up to three users, three dashboards, thirty days of data retention, no export or single sign-on, and, critically, the AI-insights feature capped at twenty queries a month with a hard cutoff rather than a soft warning, so that the single largest cost-to-serve risk in the model could never exceed a known ceiling. She paired the launch with a standing monthly review, run jointly by finance and product, of the fully loaded cost to serve the active free base against the gross margin that free tier was generating in conversions — with an explicit kill-switch: if that cost ever exceeded 25% of self-serve gross margin, the AI feature's free-tier quota would be cut further before anything else changed. The point of the kill-switch was not caution for its own sake; it was Meera's way of making sure the freemium decision remained a hypothesis that could be revisited with data, rather than a one-time bet the board would only revisit at the next crisis.

What she asked her team to study next was the deeper question the AI-insights feature had already put in front of her: how do you price a product whose marginal cost per use is no longer close to zero, the way traditional software's was, because every query now calls a metered external model — a question the field is still working out, and one this graph takes up directly under AI cost-to-serve and pricing, alongside a fuller account of how a much larger company, Dropbox, once faced a related version of exactly this free-tier question at a very different scale.

Two questions worth sitting with.

If your product's marginal cost per free user rose fivefold tomorrow — because of an AI feature, a storage-heavy use case, or simply success — would your free tier still make economic sense, and which specific feature would you cut first to protect it?

Is your free tier actually proving that people find your product valuable enough to keep using without paying, or is it only proving that people will sign up for something described as free? The two are not the same claim, and only a genuine usage cohort, tracked past the first week, tells them apart.

Netra Field Systems: The Cost of Solo

A packaging decision in Durgapur, October 2026

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Thursday, 8 October 2026, Nabanita Chatterjee was the last person on the second floor of Netra Field Systems' office in Durgapur. The board paper was due by ten next morning. The board met on Tuesday, 13 October, two days before Panchami, after which the office shut until the twenty-first.

Nabanita, Vice-President of Product, had written three versions of the same paper. Each recommended something different; each was, so far as she could tell, arithmetically correct. The question the board had asked in July was stuck to her monitor: What is the free tier costing us, and should we keep it?

The difficulty was not that nobody could answer. Three people already had. Tirthankar Basu, who ran the platform, put the cost of the free tier at ₹8.98 lakh a month. Hiranmoy Bose, who ran support, put it at ₹37.88 lakh. Bithika Majumdar, the Chief Financial Officer, put it at ₹155.35 lakh, and had said so to Fjordvik Kapital, the company's Oslo investor, in the August pack. Nabanita had spent six weeks looking for the error. There was none. Each was correctly derived from its own basis, and no arithmetic she knew would reconcile them.

2. How Netra came to give things away

Netra Field Systems began in 2019 above a spares godown. Tapan Bhaumik had spent eleven years as a service manager at a Durgapur compressor dealership, watching carbon-copy job cards dissolve in the damp. His software turned a job card into a record: serial number, fault, spare consumed, hours booked, photograph. From that followed warranty claims, annual maintenance contract renewals, scheduling, spares reordering and the invoice.

Solo was not a growth tactic but an accident of April 2020, when engineers could not travel and single-man workshops in Asansol and Bardhaman had no income. Tapan set the entry tier at zero and forgot to put it back. By then Solo was what the market knew Netra by.

Then came the decision that constrains everything now. In March 2022 Netra began a pilot with Taraazu Weighing Systems of Jamshedpur, a maker of weighbridges and industrial scales with an authorised dealer in almost every mandi town in eastern India. Taraazu wanted its warranty claims in one format; Netra wanted the dealers. The pilot became a Master Service Network Agreement, signed on 14 March 2024 and running to 31 March 2029, and to win it Tapan agreed to clause 7.3: Netra shall make available, at no charge to the dealer, a service-record level sufficient to raise warranty job cards and submit claims, to every firm holding a valid Taraazu authorisation. Clause 7.4 added a Bengali and Hindi helpdesk with a four-hour first-response commitment for the same dealers. Withdrawal of either is a material breach carrying ₹2.40 crore of liquidated damages.

In January 2025 a near-identical clause went into a smaller agreement with Sekiyama Kikai of Nagoya and its ninety-six Indian service partners. Between the two, in August 2024, Fjordvik Kapital led a Series B of ₹88 crore on a plan promising surplus by March 2027.

3. The market Netra sits in

Field-service software in India is sold into a market that has not decided whether it is buying software at all. Salesforce Field Service and SAP sit inside the IT budgets of large equipment makers; Zoho's FSM and Freshworks' service desk are bought by firms already using those vendors; and several hundred thousand service firms run on WhatsApp and a diary. Netra's competition is almost never another product. It is the diary.

Two forces push in Netra's favour: GST e-invoicing thresholds have descended far enough that a firm billing ₹5 crore must issue structured invoices, and the job card is where the line items come from; and UPI collection through Razorpay and PhonePe ended the cheque-chasing that made AMC renewals unprofitable. Against that, equipment makers — Voltas, Kirloskar, Thermax and their peers — periodically consider building a dealer portal in-house, and their dealers' willingness to pay follows AMC rates barely moved in five years.

Netra's tiers are Solo, free and capped at one engineer and forty job cards a month; Workshop at ₹900 a month; Depot at ₹2,400; Network at ₹9,000 for multi-site firms. Exhibit 2 gives the September position.

4. Three costs, all correct

The quarter produced three costings of one tier, by three functions never asked to agree.

Tirthankar's number answers what would we stop paying; Hiranmoy's, what effort does this tier consume; Bithika's, what must every account carry if we are to reach surplus. Only the third appears in the investor pack, because only it reconciles to the statutory accounts — and it makes Solo the largest single line of expenditure in the business.

5. The tail that the average hides

In July, Hiranmoy's team tagged every Solo support contact by account; Exhibit 5 is the result.

1,03,605 of the 1,26,400 Solo accounts, 82.0 per cent, raised no ticket in three months. At the other end, 290 of 1,26,400, or 0.23 per cent, raised 13,630 of the 64,950 tickets — 21.0 per cent of Solo support, and ₹13.63 lakh of the ₹64.95 lakh it cost. Widen the tail to the top two bands and 1,070 of 1,26,400 accounts, 0.85 per cent, hold 26,110 of the 64,950 tickets, or 40.2 per cent.

So the ₹29.97 average in Exhibit 3 is honest and useless: the correct mean of a distribution in which the median Solo account costs almost nothing while the 290 in the last band cost ₹4,700 each a quarter in support alone — ₹1,566.67 a month, more than Workshop brings in. Nabanita's instinct was to remove the tail. Then the tagging was matched to the dealer register: 214 of the 290 heaviest accounts, 73.8 per cent, are Taraazu authorised dealers, and clause 7.4 is why they telephone. They are expensive because Netra promised, with liquidated damages attached, that they could be.

6. Three conversion rates, all correct

What does Solo buy? Exhibit 6 takes one cohort — every account opened on Solo in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 — and one numerator, the 2,431 paying at the end. Only the denominator changes.

2,431 of 74,800 registrations, or 3.25 per cent, is what Bithika sets beside the ₹155.35 lakh, and on that pairing Solo is indefensible. 2,431 of the 18,700 accounts active in the last ninety days, 13.0 per cent, is what Tathagata Roychowdhury quotes to OEM partners, and on that pairing Solo is a well-run funnel. 2,431 of 26,180 qualified accounts, 9.29 per cent, is Nabanita's preferred figure, and she knows she prefers it because it sits in the middle.

7. The revenue nobody attributes to Solo

Netra books revenue by source line, and Exhibit 7 shows why Solo has a defender who never names it.

The OEM and dealer line is the largest, and Tathagata's bonus and the Taraazu renewal he negotiates in 2028 both rest on it. Yet when Nabanita's team traced those accounts, 4,486 of the 5,940 on that line, 75.5 per cent, had opened a Solo account before they paid — worth ₹57.79 lakh a month at the line's average billing. Read one way, three-quarters of the partner line is free-tier revenue wearing another badge. Read the other way, those firms opened Solo accounts because a dealer-network manager opened one with them, on the strength of the Taraazu contract, and would have come by another door. Exhibits 6 and 7 cannot both be taken at face value: the cohort says Solo produced the accounts, the ledger says partnerships did.

Of the 1,180 firms holding a Taraazu authorisation, 842 — 71.4 per cent — are on Solo and pay nothing; 338 pay. Sekiyama's ninety-six partners split seventy-one free, twenty-five paying.

8. The people

Nabanita Chatterjee, Vice-President of Product, Durgapur, owns the paper, and argues the board is being asked to price a channel as though it were a product. Unsaid: her ₹53.99 lakh self-serve line is the smallest of the three, and the first to shrink if registration closes.

Tapan Bhaumik, founder and Chief Executive, Durgapur, signed clause 7.3. Solo is the company's distribution, he says; closing it would be a dealer pulling down his own shutter. Unsaid: he has never read Exhibit 5.

Bithika Majumdar, Chief Financial Officer, Durgapur, carries the March 2027 surplus and wrote April's allocation policy. Only ₹155.35 lakh a month reconciles to the accounts, she says. Unsaid: the divisor is a choice, and account count showed a problem she already believed in.

Tirthankar Basu, Head of Platform Engineering, Bardhaman, made the most defensible measurement in the company and thinks the argument manufactured. Unsaid: a storage project deferred twice means ₹8.98 lakh will not hold another year.

Hiranmoy Bose, Head of Customer Support, Asansol, absorbs the tail. He objects not to free accounts but to a free tier with a four-hour contractual response and no revenue. Unsaid: his headcount is budgeted against total tickets.

Tathagata Roychowdhury, Head of OEM and Dealer Partnerships, Jamshedpur, quotes 13.0 per cent conversion and the largest source line, and warns that touching Solo endangers the Taraazu renewal. Unsaid: Taraazu's service head has twice asked what an in-house portal would cost.

Barnali Sarkar, Lead Data Analyst, Kharagpur, built Exhibit 6. No rate should be quoted without its denominator, she says. Unsaid: she flagged the ninety-day defect in May, in a comment nobody answered.

Bidisha Lahiri, Head of Enterprise and Field Sales, Ranchi, wants a thirty-day trial, because a trial gives her a deadline and free never does. Unsaid: 148 of her 1,830 accounts, billing ₹3.84 lakh a month, began as Solo registrations.

Ragnhild Hauge of Fjordvik Kapital watches from Oslo, three and a half hours behind, and cares about March 2027 more than the shape of a tier.

9. Voices

“I can give you the number that disappears if we switch Solo off tonight. It is ₹8.98 lakh. I cannot give you Bithika's number, because the engineers she charges to Solo will still be here on Monday.”

Tirthankar Basu, management meeting, 25 September 2026

“Do not put three conversion rates in one paper without three denominators beside them. If the board sees 13 per cent and then 3.25 per cent in the pack Ragnhild already has, the first question will not be about pricing.”

Barnali Sarkar, on the draft board paper, 2 October 2026

“Two hundred and ninety accounts. Forty-seven tickets each in a quarter. Every one entitled to a four-hour response in Bengali because of a clause in a contract I was not shown.”

Hiranmoy Bose, internal chat, 18 September 2026

“You are describing my dealers as a cost. They are why 5,940 paying accounts exist. Take the free level away and I am renegotiating Taraazu in the quarter I am meant to be extending it.”

Tathagata Roychowdhury, reply to Hiranmoy Bose, 18 September 2026

10. The options as Nabanita has written them

Her three drafts correspond to three courses, and Exhibit 8 projects each to a month-twelve run-rate. It assumes the metering pilot in Asansol and Bardhaman generalises, its weakest joint: over eight weeks there, new Solo registrations ran at 903 against a forecast of 1,612, a fall of 44 per cent, while 1,640 existing accounts upgraded within a month of the cap.

Subtract each course's Solo cost from its revenue and the ranking changes with the basis. On the marginal basis the figures are ₹191.43 lakh, ₹190.14 lakh and ₹187.47 lakh, and holding Solo wins. On the fully allocated basis they are ₹158.29 lakh, ₹169.14 lakh and ₹167.76 lakh, and metering wins. On the finance basis they are ₹23.64 lakh, ₹58.18 lakh and ₹185.99 lakh, and the contract-only level wins by a distance that makes the others look careless. Nothing in the arithmetic is wrong. The ranking is a function of the basis, and the basis is a choice the board delegated in April.

Course 3 inverts what everyone believes about free users. Strip out the Solo accounts no clause covers — 1,25,124 in the scenario, where all 1,276 entitled firms take the free level, or 1,25,487 today, where only 913 do — and what remains is the tail: the average fully allocated cost of a free account rises from ₹29.97 a month to ₹1,551.72, the cheap majority having subsidised the expensive minority all along. Nabanita cannot decide if that argues for Course 3 or against averages.

11. The deadline and what cannot move

The paper is due at ten on Friday, 9 October. The board sits on Tuesday, 13 October, and the office closes for Puja from the fifteenth to the twenty-first, so a decision not taken then is taken in November.

Clauses 7.3 and 7.4 run to 31 March 2029, cover all 1,180 authorised dealers, and carry ₹2.40 crore of liquidated damages; Sekiyama's agreement carries a similar obligation for the ninety-six partners whose general manager in Nagoya, Yusuke Tamai, has twice asked if it is guaranteed. Any change touching those 1,276 firms is a contract negotiation, not a pricing decision, and Netra's outside counsel advises that a job-card cap holds under 7.3 only if warranty job cards are exempt — which is precisely the tail. The Series B plan promises surplus by March 2027 against September's ₹17.71 lakh a month, and headcount is frozen until April. The DPDP Act makes bulk deletion of dormant free accounts a notification exercise, not a database command. And 1,03,605 firms that pay nothing keep their machine histories, warranty records and AMC dates inside Netra.

12. Questions

  1. Reconstruct each costing in Exhibit 3 from its own basis. Which decision is each the right input to, and which does it mislead?
  2. Exhibit 5 shows a mean of ₹29.97 across a distribution in which 82.0 per cent of accounts raise no ticket. What packaging change follows from the tail rather than the mean?
  3. All three rates in Exhibit 6 are correct. Which denominator should govern a pricing decision, and what must be true of the cohort for it to hold?
  4. Exhibits 6 and 7 disagree about who produced the OEM and dealer line. Design a measurement that would settle it, and say what Netra should have instrumented in 2024.
  5. Does clause 7.3 make Solo a product, a contract or a channel decision — and does your answer change for the 1,25,487 Solo accounts it does not cover today, or the scenario’s 1,25,124?
  6. What should Nabanita put in Friday's paper, and what should she say when Ragnhild Hauge asks which single number the free tier costs?

At half past midnight Nabanita closed the three drafts without deleting any. The note was still on the monitor. She had an answer to every question the board could ask about the free tier except the one it had asked, and three correct numbers where one was wanted, and beside her the Taraazu agreement lay open at clause 7.3, a pencil line under the words at no charge to the dealer.
case20v1-price.freemium:
Aankalan Ledger Cloud: What Stays Free

A pricing decision in Ludhiana

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Gurleen Brar, Head of Product at Aankalan Ledger Cloud, sat in the company's first-floor office in Focal Point, Ludhiana, with one slide on her laptop and eight days to the board meeting on Wednesday, 14 October. The slide had a single line: "Free tier: keep, cut or replace?" Diwali was four weeks away, when small manufacturers and traders raise invoices in bulk.

Aankalan gave away invoicing and GST return filing to any business that sent fewer than 50 invoices a month. That generosity had built a base of 1,95,000 businesses and a cost line the founder, Amarjit Dhillon, called "a second payroll". Gurleen had to bring the board one recommendation on what should stay free, and it had to survive the questions of a sales head who wanted a trial, a finance committee that wanted a saving, and a founder who did not want to lose the customers who had made the company.

2. Company background

Amarjit Dhillon founded Aankalan in 2019 after watching his family's cycle-parts workshop lose three days every month to GST paperwork. The product is cloud accounting for firms with turnover of ₹50 lakh to ₹15 crore: hosiery makers, hand-tool units, cycle-parts suppliers, and the trading firms that sell to them. It produces GST-ready invoices, tracks receivables, prepares returns and, at the higher tiers, manages stock and multiple GST registrations.

The competition is crowded. Tally Prime sits on the machines of most accountants in Punjab. Zoho Books and Vyapar sell to the same owners, ClearTax and Marg ERP to their accountants, and the GST portal run by the GST Network lets any firm file its returns at no charge, so Aankalan is always selling convenience rather than access. Its tiers are Free, Plus and Pro. Exhibit 1 shows the position at the end of September 2026.

Exhibit 1 carries the whole tension. Only 15,000 of 1,95,000 businesses pay, a share of 7.7 per cent. Yet the 1,80,000 free businesses account for ₹25.20 lakh of the ₹43.20 lakh monthly cost, or 58.3 per cent, mostly because GST return filing is expensive to support in the last week of every month.

3. The situation

Free had been a deliberate bet. In 2020 Amarjit reasoned that a Ludhiana hosiery owner would never pay for software he had not tried, and that chartered accountants, who file for dozens of clients each, would recommend whatever their clients already used. He was right about the accountants: most new sign-ups still arrive on a CA's recommendation, and that recommendation costs Aankalan nothing.

The doubts began in the summer. Sahil Grewal, a data analyst working from Surat, ran an experiment between 1 July and 30 September 2026 in which the same advertising reached two groups of 20,000 landing-page visitors. One saw the existing free tier. The other was offered a 14-day trial of Pro, after which the account turned read-only. Exhibit 2 gives the results.

The trial produced sharper users and 8 per cent more payers, 324 against 300. It also cut sign-ups by 40 per cent, from 6,000 to 3,600. Sahil's caution was that ninety days is short for a firm that renews once a year.

Colleagues read the numbers from where they sit. In Khanna, Manjot Sekhon, who runs sales and the CA partner channel, hears prospects say "free" and then never log in. In Chandigarh, Arshdeep Mann leads support and sees the free tier eating Friday afternoons. In Auckland, the contract designer Gagandeep Randhawa, working a seven-and-a-half-hour time difference from Ludhiana, points out that any GST prompt inside the free flow is a design decision as much as a pricing one.

4. The people

Amarjit Dhillon, founder and CEO, Ludhiana. He wants profitability without abandoning the customers and accountants who trusted the company.

Manjot Sekhon, Head of Sales, Khanna. He wants a trial, because his team's time is spent on leads that never intend to pay, and a deadline creates urgency.

Arshdeep Mann, Head of Support, Chandigarh. He wants free to cost less to serve, and would accept a smaller free tier if the tickets fell with it.

Sahil Grewal, Senior Analyst, Surat. He wants the decision made on the experiment, and wants the board told what the experiment cannot show.

5. The options

Gurleen framed three courses. Exhibit 3 puts each on a common monthly run-rate.

Option A: keep freemium as it is. This preserves the CA channel and the goodwill of the 1,80,000. The cost is a free tier that takes 58.3 per cent of spending, growing with every sign-up, with no lever to slow it.

Option B: replace it with a 14-day trial. Exhibit 3 shows the short-run contribution rising to ₹91.80 lakh, ₹18.00 lakh above today. The cost is what the run-rate cannot show: new sign-ups fall by 40 per cent, the CAs lose the free product they recommend, and next year's payers are drawn from a smaller pool of businesses that have already learned to keep their books on Aankalan.

Option C: narrow the free tier and trial the upgrade. Invoicing stays free up to 50 a month, together with receivables and a JSON export that any firm may upload to the GST portal's own free tool. One-click GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B filing moves to Plus, with a 14-day Plus trial offered on the day a firm first prepares a return. Exhibit 3 puts contribution at ₹90.30 lakh, ₹16.50 lakh above today and only ₹1.50 lakh below Option B, while keeping the free base intact. The cost is that the uplift of 1,500 Plus accounts is an assumption, a 10 per cent rise on 15,000 payers, slightly above the 8 per cent seen in the trial.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what does each free business cost Aankalan, and what does the free tier buy in return? What would a trial lose?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows better activation and more payers in the trial arm. Why is it still not enough to justify Option B?
  3. If the assumed 1,500 new Plus accounts in Option C do not arrive, does Option C still beat Option A? Show the arithmetic.
  4. Which single feature should be the boundary between Free and Plus, and how would you test that boundary before the board meets?

7. A note for the learner

The lens is that free is the lowest tier and it must have a purpose. A free tier that serves as habit, data and a referral channel is an acquisition cost; one that serves as a discount is a subsidy. The test for any feature is whether giving it away makes a paying customer more likely later, or merely makes the free customer content. Free versus trial is then a question of when the customer meets the value: a freemium product lets them meet it slowly and repeatedly, a trial forces a verdict inside a fortnight.

The defensible path is Option C. Invoicing is the habit and the CA-recommended entry point, and it is cheap to serve; GST return filing is the point where value peaks and cost peaks at once, so it belongs behind the price. Trial the filing, not the product, so the firm pays at the moment it feels the saving, and only after it has entered its data.

Arithmetic makes the path robust. If Plus grows by nothing, Option C still costs ₹34.20 lakh (₹16.20 lakh free, ₹12.00 lakh Plus, ₹6.00 lakh Pro) against revenue of ₹117.00 lakh, a contribution of ₹82.80 lakh, ₹9.00 lakh above Option A. The case for it does not depend on the optimistic assumption. Option B looks similar in the short run, but it spends the sign-up pool that feeds next year's payers.

Gurleen should propose Option C for a 90-day pilot beginning after Diwali, with three measures set in advance: the share of Plus upgrades among firms that prepare a return, the number of free businesses that leave, and support tickets per free business. If departures exceed the savings, she returns to the board with the evidence rather than the argument.

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Pricing & Packaging · Exp40

Freemium and the Free Trial: The Carrying Cost of an Option

Two companies, an AI-native document product in Pune and a hardware business in Ahmedabad, reach the same question from opposite directions: how long are you willing to hold an option on a user who has not paid you, and what does holding it cost? The answer turns out to depend far less on the cloud bill than almost everyone in the room believes.

1. Two rooms, October and November 2025

On the afternoon of 14 October 2025, in a converted bungalow off Baner Road in Pune, Aparna Ravindran put a single slide on the wall of Chitralekha Systems' fourth-floor meeting room and left it there for the better part of two hours. Chitralekha sold contract and document intelligence to mid-market legal and procurement teams: upload a master services agreement, a distribution contract or a stack of vendor paper, and the product returned a clause-level review, a deviation report against the customer's own playbook, and a searchable repository. It had 640 paying accounts, an average contract value of ₹2,40,000 a year, gross margin of 72% after inference and infrastructure, and a monthly logo churn of 2.9%. It had grown for four years on a fourteen-day free trial with 500 document credits, which produced about 410 trial starts a month and converted 9% of them.

The slide said: Free tier: go or no go. Behind it sat six months of pilot data from a permanently free version Chitralekha had quietly shipped in July to traffic from three southern metros, and a finance model built by Girish Salunke, the chief financial officer, that had already been rewritten four times. Every previous version of the argument had turned on the same number: the cost of inference. A full review of a thirty-page agreement cost Chitralekha about ₹34 in tokens once retrieval, a long-context reasoning pass and a verification pass were counted. Salunke's position, stated in writing in August, was that a free tier in a product with a real marginal cost per use was a standing subsidy with no natural ceiling, and that Chitralekha would be buying growth with gross margin it could not spare. Tara Menon, who ran growth from Bengaluru, held the opposite view with equal force: the trial reached only buyers already searching for contract review software, a population Chitralekha had nearly exhausted, and the pilot had lifted signups 3.1 times without a rupee of extra media spend.

What Ravindran eventually put in front of the two of them was not a number about inference at all. It was the observation that in the pilot's first cohort, the monthly probability that an active free account converted had fallen from 1.4% in its first month to 0.22% by its sixth, and stayed there. Once that was on the whiteboard, the inference argument collapsed — not because it was wrong, but because it was second order. This page is, in large part, an explanation of why.

Three hundred and fifty kilometres north-west, on 6 November 2025, Devendra Pathak was making a different version of the same argument to the board of Chandrabhaga Devices in Ahmedabad. Chandrabhaga made three-phase energy monitors for small manufacturing units — textile processing houses in Surat, forging shops in Rajkot, pump makers around Coimbatore — and sold them outright at ₹18,500 a unit against a hardware gross margin of 38%, or ₹7,030 per device. Since 2017 the box had carried a printed line: lifetime access to the Chandrabhaga app, free. There were 41,000 devices in the field across 9,300 sites, and 14,200 of them were more than five years old.

Pathak's problem was not acquisition. It was that the free app had grown teeth. Customers now wanted one-second sampling so that the monitor could catch voltage sags and harmonic distortion events — the failures that actually destroyed motors — and one-second sampling took the fully loaded cost of ingesting, storing and serving a single device's telemetry from ₹31 a month to ₹96. Ila Bhagat, the chief financial officer, had done the division in a single line of a spreadsheet and circulated it without comment: ₹7,030 divided by ₹96 is 73 months. A Chandrabhaga device sold in 2019 would, in the second half of 2025, consume the last rupee of the gross margin it had earned, and then keep consuming. The devices had a service life of eight to ten years. The free tier, in other words, had a maturity date, and it had been knowable at the moment of sale for eight years without anyone having calculated it.

Chitralekha and Chandrabhaga are useful together precisely because their economics point in opposite directions. For Chitralekha, free access has a real, metered, per-use cost and no contractual promise attached. For Chandrabhaga, free access costs relatively little per unit but is bound by a promise printed on a box, attached to a physical good that will outlive several product roadmaps. Both are asking what should stay free. Neither can answer it with the standard framing.

2. The idea, stated precisely, and the five camps that disagree about it

The working definitions are not in dispute. A free trial is bounded access — by time, by usage, or by both — that terminates. A freemium model is a permanently available version of the product that a user may keep indefinitely without paying, alongside a paid version that delivers more. The distinction that matters for an expert is not about duration but about who holds the option and for how long.

Think of every non-paying user as an option the vendor has written. The vendor pays a carrying cost every period the user remains on the books, and holds the right to a payoff if and when the user converts. A trial is an option with a fixed, short expiry: cheap to carry, certain to resolve, and it resolves whether or not the user has learned enough to decide. Freemium is a perpetual option: expensive to carry in aggregate, never forced to resolve, and — this is the part that is routinely missed — it is also an option the user holds on the vendor's future improvements. In a fast-improving category, a rational free user waits, because waiting is free and the product keeps getting better. That single asymmetry does more damage to freemium conversion in AI-era products than any cost line in the model.

Where the idea came from

The deep ancestor is shareware, not marketing. In 1982 Andrew Fluegelman distributed PC-Talk with a request for voluntary payment; Jim Button and Bob Wallace followed with PC-File and PC-Write. What those men were solving was a distribution problem in a world where the marginal cost of a floppy disk was real: they could not afford to give the artefact away, so they gave away the copy and asked for the money afterwards. Their successors invented crippleware and demoware — deliberately maimed versions — and by the mid-1990s the time-boxed evaluation copy was the industry standard, because software was a good you shipped and evaluation was a cost you wanted bounded.

The economics changed when delivery moved to the network. Netscape's 1994 decision to make Navigator free for individual use is usually told as a browser-war story; it is better read as the first large demonstration that when marginal distribution cost approaches zero, giving the artefact away permanently can be the cheapest possible way to reach a market. The word "freemium" arrived in 2006, coined by Jarid Lukin of Alacra in a comment on a post by the venture investor Fred Wilson, who was describing what he then saw working at Skype and Flickr. Chris Anderson's Free (2009) turned it into a general theory of abundance; Malcolm Gladwell's review of that book in The New Yorker the same year is still the most useful published statement of the case against, because it insisted that "free" is never free, only differently funded, and asked who is actually paying. Vineet Kumar's 2014 Harvard Business Review piece, "Making Freemium Work," is the first widely read practitioner treatment that puts the free tier's design — how much you give, to whom, for how long — ahead of the decision to have one. The formal literature on when free-with-upgrade beats time-limited seeding, most usefully Niculescu and Wu's work in Information Systems Research, converges on a result practitioners rarely state: the choice depends less on the product's quality than on the shape of how users learn its value over time.

That sentence is the argument of this page, and it is why the Exp20 treatment — which correctly identifies cost-to-serve as the thing early-stage teams underweight — is only half the story. Cost-to-serve determines whether a free tier is affordable. The learning curve of value determines whether it works at all.

The five camps

An experienced product manager refereeing an argument about free tiers is almost always refereeing a collision between two of the following five positions, and the fastest way to make progress is to name them out loud. Each is intellectually respectable. Each will sign some propositions and refuse others, and the refusals are more diagnostic than the endorsements.

Table 1 — Five schools of thought on what should stay free. The right-hand column is the useful one: it is what each camp will not concede even under pressure.
SchoolCore proposition it will signWhat it rests onWhat it refuses to sign
Distribution
(Wilson; the product-led growth tradition)		 The free tier is a marketing channel. Judge it against the paid acquisition budget it displaces, not against its own gross margin. Observed CAC collapse in products where the user is the buyer; the durability of installed bases built free. That the free tier should be profitable standalone, or that free users who never convert are waste.
Versioning
(Shapiro and Varian; Deneckere and McAfee on damaged goods)		 Free is the bottom rung of a self-selection menu. The only question is whether the damage you inflict sorts buyers correctly. Second-degree price discrimination theory; the observed success of gating on seats, administration and compliance rather than on core quality. That you should give away your most valuable capability to drive adoption. Generosity on the wrong axis is a tax on your own price.
Network
(Katz and Shapiro; marketplace and platform operators)		 Free exists to build installed base, liquidity or content. A free user who never pays can be worth more than one who does. Direct and indirect network effects; the empirical failure of marketplaces that charged the thin side early. That the free side should be measured by conversion rate. For them that metric is a category error.
Information
(enterprise sales leadership; the trial tradition)		 The purpose of free access is to resolve uncertainty and produce a decision. Decisions need deadlines; information has a half-life. Deal-cycle data showing that evaluations without an end date do not end; the observed anchoring damage of open-ended free access in negotiated sales. That a buyer should be allowed to stay free indefinitely. They regard the perpetual free tier as a refusal to ask for the order.
Carrying cost
(the finance view, ascendant since 2022)		 The free base is an inventory position. It has a carrying cost per unit per period, and that cost must be bounded and falling. Cloud and inference bills that scaled with free usage rather than revenue; the 2022–24 repricing of growth-at-any-cost. That the free tier's cost is a strategic investment beyond scrutiny. They want a budget, an owner and a ceiling.

Salunke at Chitralekha was arguing from the carrying-cost camp and Menon from the distribution camp, which is why they had been talking past each other for three months: neither position is falsifiable by the other's evidence. Ravindran's contribution was to move the argument onto versioning ground, where both sets of evidence become relevant to the same question. At Chandrabhaga the collision was different — Pathak was arguing from network and installed-base logic, Bhagat from carrying cost, and the promise on the box meant that the information camp's preferred instrument, an expiry, was unavailable to either of them.

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic experts actually run

There is a closed-form treatment of this decision, it takes about fifteen minutes to set up, and in the author's experience fewer than one team in five has run it. It is worth working through in full, because the structure of the formula — specifically, which term sits in the numerator and which in the denominator — is what tells you where to look.

The free base as a reservoir

Model the population of active free accounts as a stock fed by signups and drained by two exits. Let s be monthly signups, c the monthly hazard that an active free account converts to paid, d the monthly hazard that it goes dormant or is deleted, m the fully loaded cost of serving one active free account for one month, V the present value of gross profit from an account at the moment it converts, and r a monthly discount rate.

The steady-state population is F* = s / (c + d). More usefully, the expected present value that one free signup creates is

Nfree = ( c V − m ) / ( c + d + r ) Expected discounted time spent in the free state is 1/(c+d+r). During that time the account costs m per month and converts at rate c, each conversion worth V.

Two structural facts follow immediately, and both are routinely missed. First, the sign of a free account's value depends only on the numerator: a free tier creates value if and only if c V > m. The denominator scales the magnitude but cannot change the direction. Second — and this is the one that reliably surprises growth teams — reducing free-user churn d only helps if cV exceeds m. If your free tier is value-destroying at the margin, keeping free users alive longer makes it worse. Every re-engagement campaign aimed at dormant free accounts is a bet that you already know the sign of the numerator, and most teams running those campaigns have never computed it.

The trial has a simpler expression, because it resolves too fast for discounting to matter. With q the trial conversion rate, mT the monthly cost of a trial user and T the trial length in months:

Ntrial = q V − mT T Note that mT is usually much larger than m. Trial users binge; free users graze.

Chitralekha's numbers, worked

Chitralekha's paying accounts generate ₹2,40,000 a year at 72% gross margin, or ₹14,400 a month of gross profit. At 2.9% monthly logo churn and a 1% monthly discount rate, the value of a converted account is ₹14,400 / 0.039 = ₹3,69,231. Trial users consumed a mean of 62 documents during their fourteen days, at ₹34 a document, so mTT = ₹2,108. With q = 9%:

Ntrial = 0.09 × 3,69,231 − 2,108 = ₹33,231 − ₹2,108 = ₹31,123 per trial start. At 410 starts a month, the trial creates about ₹1.28 crore a month of expected lifetime gross profit.

The pilot free tier — ten documents a month, one seat, no integrations — produced, after six months, a stabilised conversion hazard of 0.22% a month and a dormancy hazard of 11%. Mean cost to serve was ₹100 a month (₹82 of inference on a mean of 2.4 documents, ₹18 of storage and platform).

Nfree = (0.0022 × 3,69,231 − 100) / (0.0022 + 0.11 + 0.01) = (812 − 100) / 0.1222 = ₹5,829 per free signup.

For freemium to beat the trial at the whole-funnel level, the signup multiplier must exceed 31,123 / 5,829 = 5.34×. The pilot delivered 3.1×. On these numbers the free tier loses, and loses clearly.

Now run the sensitivity that Salunke had been demanding for three months. Suppose inference cost per document falls from ₹34 to ₹9 — a plausible two-year move given what happened to the cost of equivalent capability between 2023 and 2025. Mean cost to serve drops from ₹100 to about ₹40. Recompute: Nfree = (812 − 40) / 0.1222 = ₹6,317. The required multiplier falls from 5.34× to 4.93×. A 60% reduction in cost to serve moves the decision by eight percent. The entire inference argument, which had consumed a quarter of executive attention, was worth less than a rounding error in the conversion hazard.

The reason is visible in the formula. cV = ₹812 and m = ₹100. Cost is a sixth of the numerator. The binding variable is c, and c is not a fact about the market; it is a consequence of where the free line is drawn.

The step that is almost always left implicit: the price tax

Here is the second calculation that expert practitioners run and that appears in almost no internal deck. Consider two segments: a low-value user — a solo in-house counsel reviewing eight contracts a month — with value vL for the full product, and a high-value buyer — a twelve-person legal operations team at a listed manufacturer — with value vH. Let θ denote the fraction of a user's value that the free version already delivers to that user. For the high-value buyer to pay price p rather than simply use the free tier, we need vH − p ≥ θH vH, which rearranges to:

p ≤ (1 − θH) · vH The price you can charge your best customer is capped by how much of their value you have already given away for nothing.

This is the whole of the versioning school in one line, and it has a sharp design implication. θ is not a single number; it is segment-specific. The objective is to make θL as close to 1 as possible and θH as close to 0 as possible: give the solo user nearly everything they want, and the enterprise buyer nearly nothing they need. That is why single sign-on, audit logging, role-based administration, data residency, named support and integration with a system of record are such durable gates. A solo user does not care about any of them; a company with a security review cannot deploy without them. And it is why gating on core quality or on raw volume is a design error: those levers push θL and θH down together, suppressing adoption without protecting price.

At Chitralekha this was measurable. In the pilot geography, new-business ACV fell from ₹2,40,000 to ₹2,11,000 against a matched control — a 12% compression, driven entirely by the fact that Chitralekha's cost-shaped free tier gave away the clause-level review engine itself, merely in small quantities. Apply 12% to the full ₹15.36 crore book and you get ₹1.84 crore of ARR, or roughly ₹1.33 crore a year of gross profit. The steady-state cost of carrying the entire free base under the design Chitralekha eventually chose was ₹1.29 crore a year. The price tax was slightly larger than the cloud bill everybody had been arguing about, and it appeared in no version of the model.

The step after that: cost-to-serve is a distribution, not a number

The mean of ₹100 a month concealed something. Chitralekha's pilot base was radically skewed: the median free account reviewed two documents a month, the mean 2.4, and the top one percent — accounts that had discovered they could create additional workspaces and drive the product from a scraped browser session — averaged 210. Five percent of accounts consumed two-thirds of the free tier's inference bill.
