4. When the idea applies, stated as claims you can test

The conditions under which a perpetual free tier beats a trial can be written as five testable propositions. Each is applied below to both protagonists.

Claim 1: value is learned slowly, so the decision cannot be forced. The test is the shape of the conversion hazard, not its level. If most of the eventual conversion probability is concentrated in the first fortnight, a trial captures it at a fraction of the carrying cost. If the hazard has a long, flat tail — the pattern Phil Libin at Evernote memorably described as a smile, where conversion probability rises with tenure — a trial systematically destroys value by closing the option before the user has learned enough. Chitralekha: the buyer-gated cohort's hazard was flat at 0.9% out to month twelve, which satisfies the claim; the cost-gated cohort's decayed to near zero, which fails it. Chandrabhaga: the claim is close to irrelevant, because value is learned during the first electrical fault, whenever that occurs, and the customer has already paid for hardware.

Claim 2: the user is the buyer, or can become the buyer's advocate. A free tier works by accumulating individuals; it converts when one of those individuals can either authorise spend or credibly ask for it. The test is the share of converted accounts in which the person who signed up is the person who paid, or invited the person who paid, within ninety days. Below about a third, the free tier is producing enthusiasm without a path. Chitralekha: 71% of pilot conversions came from accounts where a second user on the same email domain had been invited first, which is a strong pass. Chandrabhaga: fails outright — the app user is a plant electrician and the buyer is a promoter or works manager, and the two do not talk about software.

Claim 3: the free tier can be gated on an axis the enterprise needs and the individual does not. The test is Figure 3: name the top three things your free tier withholds and ask, of each, whether a solo user would notice. Chitralekha: passes in its revised design (one editor, no audit trail, no system-of-record integration), fails in its original one (document count). Chandrabhaga: passes unusually well, because the things a multi-site group needs — cross-plant rollup, statutory energy-audit report formats, ISO 50001 export, API access for the enterprise resource planning system — are invisible to a single shop floor.

Claim 4: carrying cost per account is bounded above and falling. Not "low" — bounded, meaning there exists a rupee figure no single free account can exceed in a month, and that figure is enforced by the system rather than by a policy document. Chitralekha: failed until the ceiling was built; passes now. Chandrabhaga: fails on the second half. Per-device cost was rising, not falling, because customers were asking for higher sampling rates.

Claim 5: you can live with the consequences forever. Free tiers ratchet. The test is to write, before launch, the memo you would send if you had to halve the free tier in eighteen months, and to identify who receives it. Chitralekha: passes — the pilot was explicitly labelled a pilot, with an end date, in the product itself. Chandrabhaga: catastrophically fails, and had failed in 2017, because the promise was printed on a physical box that customers still possess.

Where the idea is actively misleading. Three situations recur. The first is a product whose value is obvious in ten minutes and whose purchase requires a procurement process: here a free tier adds nothing to the buyer's information and subtracts from the seller's leverage. The second is any product where the free tier's population cannot be distinguished from the paid population by any observable characteristic — if you genuinely cannot find an axis on which θH is low, freemium is not a strategy, it is a discount you have not admitted to. The third, and least discussed, is a category where a competitor can match your free tier within a quarter. Going free is a commitment device: it is credible precisely because it is hard to reverse. In a category where everyone can commit, everyone does, and the reference price for the whole category moves to zero. Indian consumer telecom after 2016 and the zero-merchant-discount-rate regime on UPI payments are both instructive here, for opposite reasons: one was a competitive race, the other a regulatory mandate, and in both cases the question of who funds the free layer has outlived the decision that created it.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies and the free-tier arbitrage

Chitralekha sold two things: Review, the clause engine, and Vault, the repository. Each had been given its own free tier by its own product team, at different times, on different logic. Within four months of the second launch, the growth team found that 340 accounts were running the full workflow — review in Review's free tier, storage and search in Vault's free tier, with a manual export between them — assembling for nothing a combination Chitralekha sold for ₹2,40,000. The generic failure is that free tiers compose, and nobody owns the composition. Mature multi-product companies handle this with a single free-tier policy owned above the product lines, specifying which gates are global (seats, administration, audit) and which are local. What they say they do is design each product's free tier around its own users; what they actually do, after the first arbitrage incident, is centralise the gates that touch identity and administration and let the rest vary.

Two-sided markets, where conversion is the wrong metric entirely

Chausar Networks, a Coimbatore marketplace matching original-equipment buyers to computer-numerical-control machine shops, lets shops list capacity free and charges buyers a 4.5% take rate. In its 2025 financial year it carried 6,800 listed shops of which 1,900 were active, intermediated ₹410 crore of gross merchandise value, and earned ₹18.45 crore of take. Cost to serve a free shop — verification, capability survey, support, periodic re-audit — ran to ₹190 a month, or ₹1.55 crore a year across the base.

A conversion-rate framing of Chausar's free side yields approximately zero, and this is by design: shops are never meant to pay. The metric that governs the free side is cell density. Chausar's matching only works when a capability-and-region cell — say, five-axis milling within 200 kilometres of Pune — contains at least about 120 verified shops; below that, buyers submit a requirement, receive two quotes, and leave. In 2025, 61% of Chausar's cells cleared the threshold. The free side's budget is therefore a market-making budget, and the correct question about it is not "what is the conversion rate" but "what does the marginal rupee of free-side spend do to the share of cells above threshold". The twist Chausar discovered in mid-2025 is the one that eventually bites every marketplace with a free supply side: an internal audit found that 22% of free-listed shops had transacted with a buyer they first met on Chausar and then invoiced directly, leakage worth roughly ₹2.6 crore of foregone take. The instinct is to start charging shops. The correct move, which Chausar took, is to make the paid side stickier — escrow, inspection, and a warranty on first articles — so that transacting off-platform costs the buyer something.

Regulated products, where free users are not cheap

Chitrakoot Health Cloud, a Hyderabad company selling clinical documentation software to small hospitals, ran a free tier for single-doctor practices for two years before its counsel ended it. The reasoning generalises. In regulated domains, a free user carries the same obligations as a paying one: under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, consent, notice, breach notification and erasure duties do not scale with revenue; a clinical decision-support feature carries the same liability exposure whether or not money changed hands; and in financial services, a free tier that offers anything resembling advice can pull a firm inside the perimeter of the Securities and Exchange Board of India's research-analyst or investment-adviser regulations. The instructive contrast is Zerodha, which has run one of the cleanest feature-gated free tiers in Indian financial services for a decade — zero brokerage on equity delivery, a flat fee on intraday and derivatives — precisely because the free thing and the paid thing are separated along a regulatory-clean line that also happens to be a willingness-to-pay line. That is not luck; it is what good gating looks like in a regulated market.

Hardware plus software, where the free tier has a maturity date

Chandrabhaga's situation is the general one for connected hardware and it is under-analysed. When software is given away with a physical good, the free tier's total cost is bounded not by user behaviour but by the device's service life, and it can be computed at the moment of sale. Divide hardware gross margin by monthly cost to serve and you get the month in which the sale becomes gross-margin negative.

The point the figure makes, and that the pricing literature largely misses, is that cost to serve is an engineering variable, not an exogenous fact. Product teams treat it as given and reach for gating; infrastructure teams treat it as a cost-optimisation project with no pricing consequence. The seam between them is where most of the value sits. Chandrabhaga's adaptive-sampling change bought more relief than any plausible re-gating, and cost one engineer a quarter.

AI-native products, and the one gate where cost and willingness to pay align

The genuinely new problem is that in an AI-native product the two gating principles conflict. Figure 3's advice is to gate on axes the enterprise needs and the individual does not. But the only axes that control inference cost — volume, model quality, context length, tool calls — are precisely the axes on which the individual's value lives. Capping documents lowers θL, which is exactly what you do not want.

Three responses are being tried in the field, and none is settled. The first is capacity rationing rather than feature gating: the free user gets the whole job done, but on a smaller model, in a longer queue, at lower priority. This preserves θL at the cost of raising θH, since large organisations are often willing to be slow. The second is usage caps set generously but enforced absolutely, with a hard per-account ceiling — the Chitralekha answer — accepting the θL hit and compensating with a reverse trial that restores a forcing event. The third, and the most interesting, is to gate on automation: programmatic access, batch runs, scheduled pipelines and agentic loops. This is the single axis on which cost and willingness to pay genuinely align, because the customer who wants to run ten thousand documents unattended is both the expensive customer and the one who can obviously afford to pay. Chitralekha's final free tier gates on exactly this: a human may review as much as they like within a generous monthly ceiling; a script may not review anything at all.

The organisational seam

In every company of any size, the free tier is owned by nobody and paid for by four departments. Growth owns signups and is measured on them. Finance owns cost of goods sold and sees a line item. Support owns a queue that free users enter. Security owns the abuse. Sales owns the deals that free access complicates. No one has a profit-and-loss statement for the free tier, a budget for it, or the authority to change it. The predictable result is accretion: the free tier grows by a series of individually sensible local decisions and is never re-examined until a bill arrives. What mature companies say they do is run the free tier as a strategic investment. What they actually do, in the cases the author has seen up close, is create a named owner and a monthly free-tier gross-margin review after the first cloud-bill shock, and then maintain it for about eighteen months before attention drifts.

6. Nine things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

First: the expert asks for the hazard curve before the conversion rate. A competent practitioner reports that the free tier converts at 4%. An expert asks over what period, and then asks for conversion probability by tenure month, because a 4% rate arising from a spike in month one and a 4% rate arising from a flat 0.35% a month for a year imply opposite decisions. The tell in the wild is a pricing review where someone asks, unprompted, "is that hazard flat?" The obvious reading — that a higher conversion rate is better — is wrong because the rate is a function of the observation window, and teams choose windows that flatter them.

Second: the expert knows that the free tier is priced into the paid price, not just into the cloud bill. A team that can recite cost-to-serve to the rupee but has never estimated the compression its free tier imposes on achievable ACV is measuring the smaller of two numbers. At Chitralekha the price tax slightly exceeded the entire carrying cost. The tell is a pricing deck with a cost-to-serve slide and no matched-control ACV comparison. The obvious reading — that the free tier's cost is what it costs to run — is wrong because the largest cost of a free tier is usually the revenue it stops you charging.

Third: the expert gates on the buyer, not on the bill. When a free tier is limited by something that appears on the vendor's invoice from its cloud provider — compute minutes, documents, storage, tokens — that is cost-shaped gating, and it is almost always the wrong axis, because it is chosen for the vendor's convenience rather than for its sorting power. The tell is a free tier whose limits map one-to-one onto the vendor's own unit costs. The obvious reading — that capping the expensive thing is prudent — is wrong because it caps the thing that creates value for everyone and withholds nothing specifically from the buyer with money.

Fourth: the expert treats cost to serve as something to engineer, not something to accept. Chandrabhaga's adaptive sampling halved a cost that its product team had spent six months trying to gate around. The tell is a pricing discussion in which someone from infrastructure is present and is asked, early, what the cost would be if they had a quarter to work on it. The obvious reading — that cost to serve is an input to the pricing decision — is wrong because it is jointly determined with it.

Fifth: the expert reads the cost distribution, not the mean. In every free tier the author has examined, the top one to five percent of accounts consume between a quarter and two-thirds of the total. The tell is a practitioner who asks for the ninety-ninth percentile and then asks whether the ceiling is enforced in code or in policy. The obvious reading — that reducing average cost per free user is the goal — is wrong because the average is not where the risk lives; a single automated abuser can cost more than ten thousand ordinary users.

Sixth: the expert knows the free tier is a ratchet and writes the grandfathering policy first. You can tighten limits for new signups almost silently. You can almost never tighten them for the installed base without a public cost. The tell is a launch document that already contains a named legacy cohort, a change-of-terms clause and a memo template. The obvious reading — that terms of service give you the right to change the free tier — is wrong because the constraint is reputational rather than legal, and the reputational cost falls disproportionately on your most vocal users, who are disproportionately free.

Seventh: the expert instruments the hand-off, not the upgrade. In business software, a free account rarely converts; it is converted, by someone other than the person who signed up. The relevant events are the second user invited from the same domain, the first shared artefact, the first request routed to an administrator. The tell is a growth dashboard whose primary conversion leading indicator is "second seat invited" rather than "upgrade page viewed". The obvious reading — that you should optimise the upgrade flow — is wrong when the blocker is a procurement process the individual user cannot enter.

Eighth: the expert treats abuse as a design input rather than an operations problem. Any free tier with a real unit cost will be farmed: resold through wrappers, driven by scripts, registered at volume with disposable addresses. The tell is a free tier whose rate limits were specified by the security team in the original design document, not added in an incident review. The obvious reading — that abuse is a small percentage — is wrong because abuse concentrates in exactly the tail that dominates cost, and because the emergency response to it always damages legitimate users.

Ninth: the expert distinguishes what the free base proves from what it is used to claim. A large free base is strong evidence about activation, habit and the shape of demand at a price of zero. It is not evidence about willingness to pay for anything, and it is especially not evidence about willingness to pay for something not yet built. The tell is a practitioner who uses free-tier usage histograms to calibrate paid limits and value metrics — which is exactly what that data is good for — and who reaches for a separate study when the question is price. The obvious reading — that millions of users must indicate monetisable value — is wrong because the free base was selected on its willingness to accept a price of zero.

And a tenth, for completeness: the expert notices when free users are rationally waiting. In a category improving fast enough that this quarter's paid feature becomes next quarter's free one, the free tier teaches users that patience is profitable, and the conversion hazard falls for reasons that have nothing to do with the product's quality. The tell is a hazard curve that declines in step with your own release cadence. The remedy is not a better upgrade prompt; it is a credible commitment about what will never become free.

7. How it differs by product type and by company stage — and where it does not

Begin with what does not differ, because the literature over-segments. The reservoir arithmetic of Figure 1 is identical everywhere. The gating taxonomy is identical everywhere. The ratchet is identical everywhere, in consumer and enterprise alike. The fat-tailed cost distribution appears in every free tier that has any variable cost at all. Claims about how "B2B freemium is completely different" usually reduce to differences in the parameter values, not in the model.

What genuinely differs is the existence of a second monetisation route. In consumer software, the free tier can frequently be monetised without conversion — through advertising, or through the free user's contribution to a network that paying users value. When this is true the freemium-versus-trial question dissolves, because m becomes negative and the sign condition cV > m holds trivially. The correct framing for such a business is not "how do we convert free users" but "we run two businesses, and conversion is the smaller one."

In business software sold bottom-up, the free tier's real output is not conversion but organisational penetration: how many distinct employer domains contain at least one active free user, and how many contain three. This is the number that predicts pipeline, and it is the number that an acquirer will ask for. Conversion follows domain density with a lag of two to four quarters.

In enterprise software sold top-down, the perpetual free tier is usually wrong and the trial usually right, with one important exception: open core. When the free artefact is governed by a licence rather than by a plan, the free tier stops being a pricing decision and becomes a community contract, with contributors, forks and an ecosystem that has standing to object to changes. The relicensing controversies that have periodically swept the infrastructure-software world are, structurally, free-tier retraction events in which the ratchet had extra teeth.

In platforms and marketplaces, as Chausar shows, the free side is a market-making budget and conversion is the wrong metric. The specific risk is that the free side becomes the whole market: if the subsidised side captures enough of the surplus, the paying side never develops, and the platform discovers it has built a public good.

In hardware, the free tier is an annuity liability attached to a one-time revenue event, with a maturity set by service life. The correct instrument is a written, dated commitment at the point of sale — "included for sixty months, renewable at a published price" — which is both more honest and, in Chandrabhaga's testing with distributors in Rajkot and Surat, essentially free of effect on hardware conversion, because buyers of capital equipment are entirely accustomed to annual maintenance contracts.

In AI-native products, the free tier is a bet on a cost curve, a source of evaluation data, and a magnet for abuse, all at once, and the practice is changing fast enough that anything written here should be treated as provisional.

By stage, the pattern is consistent and under-appreciated. Pre-product-market-fit, the trial wins almost always, not for economic reasons but for informational ones: a founder needs conversations with people facing a deadline, and a free tier produces silence. At Series A and B, the reservoir is the binding constraint — a free base is a standing draw on a runway measured in months, and the reason so many seed-stage founders are attracted to freemium is that the carrying cost arrives two years after the decision. At scale, the free tier becomes affordable and simultaneously becomes a moat, because a competitor must now overcome an installed base rather than a product. At public-company scale it becomes a gross-margin line that analysts ask about, which is why the 2022–24 re-rating of software growth produced a visible wave of free-tier tightening across the industry — Heroku's removal of free dynos in late 2022 being the most-discussed instance, and one whose aftermath is still cited by every team arguing against a free tier.

8. Three worked examples

Chandanvan Learning: the free tier that pays for itself

Chandanvan Learning, based in Kochi, sells competitive-examination preparation to candidates for state and central government recruitment. By March 2025 it had 4.1 million registered accounts, 860,000 monthly active free users, and 38,000 paying subscribers at ₹4,800 a year. On the face of it, a 4.4% conversion of monthly actives — unremarkable. The interesting arithmetic is elsewhere. Chandanvan's free tier carries advertising and sponsored-listing revenue worth ₹6.20 per monthly active user per month; cost to serve, dominated by video delivery to cheap Android handsets on patchy connections, runs to ₹2.10. The free tier therefore contributes ₹4.10 per active user per month of gross margin before a single conversion — ₹35.3 lakh a month, or ₹4.2 crore a year.

Put that into the formula. With m = −₹4.10 (negative, because the free user is profitable), a monthly conversion hazard of 0.31% and a converted subscriber worth ₹9,100 of lifetime gross profit, cV − m = ₹28.20 + ₹4.10 = ₹32.30 per active user per month. There is no version of this decision in which Chandanvan should prefer a trial. The general lesson: where a second monetisation route exists, the free tier is not an acquisition cost at all and the entire freemium-versus-trial debate is a category error. The trap Chandanvan must watch is the opposite one — advertising revenue that makes the free tier so comfortable that no one ever improves the paid product.

Chausar Networks: the free side as market-making spend

Chausar's numbers appear above. What makes it a worked example rather than an anecdote is a specific decision taken in June 2025. Faced with ₹1.55 crore a year of free-side cost and ₹2.6 crore of leakage, the finance function proposed a ₹1,500 a month listing fee for shops, modelling ₹8.2 crore of new revenue at an assumed 60% retention of listed shops. The product team's counter-model asked what a 40% reduction in listed shops would do to cell density: the share of cells above the 120-shop matching threshold would fall from 61% to 34%, and buyer requirement-to-quote conversion, which Chausar tracked at 71% in dense cells and 22% in thin ones, would fall correspondingly. Applied to gross merchandise value, the listing fee would have earned ₹8.2 crore and destroyed roughly ₹14 crore of take. The fee was not introduced. In a two-sided market, the price of the free side is set by the liquidity threshold, and the threshold must be measured before the price can be argued about.

Chinar Collab: how it fails, and what recovery actually looks like

Chinar Collab, in Gurugram, sold collaborative whiteboarding and diagramming to product and engineering teams. In mid-2023 it had 2,900 paying teams, ₹22 crore of ARR, a Starter plan at ₹350 per user per month, a Business plan at ₹700, and a median paying team of nine seats. Growth was 62% year on year and decelerating. In October 2023, after a board discussion that leaned heavily on the distribution school, Chinar launched a free tier: unlimited members, three boards, unlimited history, every core feature, gated on board count, single sign-on and administrative controls.

The top-line result was spectacular. Monthly signups went from 3,100 to 16,200, a 5.2× lift, and by March 2024 the free base stood at 148,000 accounts. Four things then happened at once.

First, cannibalisation. Three boards covered 71% of what a median Starter team actually used. Within two quarters, 640 Starter teams — 19% of the Starter book — downgraded, taking ₹2.42 crore of ARR with them. Chinar had never run the one diagnostic that would have caught this: a histogram of existing low-tier customers' usage against the proposed free limits.

Second, price compression. "Unlimited members" gave away the single dimension most strongly correlated with willingness to pay. New-business ACV fell 23%. Enterprise discounting, which had averaged 14%, rose to 31%, because procurement teams now opened negotiations by observing that the product was free.

Third, cost. Mean cost to serve was a benign ₹64 an account a month, but a small population of accounts had begun embedding public boards in high-traffic websites; the ninety-ninth percentile was ₹1,900. Two percent of accounts generated 41% of a ₹1.34 crore annual bill.

Fourth, and decisively, ARR growth decelerated from 62% to 29% year on year, even as signups rose fivefold. The company had bought volume with price.

The recovery, which ran from April 2024 to June 2025, is more instructive than the failure. Chinar first tried the obvious fix: in May 2024 it reduced the free tier from three boards to two. The reversal came eleven days later, after a public backlash that reached the company's largest customers. That failure established the constraint everything else had to work within: the mistake could not be undone, only isolated.

What Chinar actually did was this. It grandfathered all 148,000 existing free accounts permanently and publicly, accepting a legacy cohort as a sunk cost. It changed the free tier for new signups to three editors with unlimited boards — inverting the gating axis from artefact count to seats, so that θL rose and θH collapsed. It installed a per-account bandwidth ceiling enforced in code. It reintroduced a fourteen-day full-feature reverse trial at the top of the free experience, restoring a forcing event without restoring a wall. It retired the Starter plan entirely and raised Business by 24%, which moved the discount floor back up. And it created a monthly free-tier gross-margin review with a single named owner in the finance organisation.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings, and the price of catching them late

The hazard that decays to nothing. The early warning is that the month-six cohort's conversion hazard is below a third of the month-one hazard. The diagnostic question is: plot conversion probability by tenure month, not conversion rate by signup month — is the tail flat? Caught early, you re-gate. Caught late, you hold a reservoir you can neither monetise nor drain, because everyone in it is grandfathered.

Cost-shaped gating. The early warning is paid ACV drifting down while free signups rise — a combination that most dashboards actively hide, because the two numbers live on different slides. The diagnostic: what does our free tier deny a 200-person buyer that it does not deny a solo user? If the honest answer is "less of the same thing", the gate is cost-shaped. Caught late, you have permanent ACV compression of 10–25%, recoverable only through a repricing event that costs churn.

The fat tail. The early warning is a ratio of ninety-ninth-percentile to mean cost above about ten. The diagnostic: what is the maximum rupee amount a single free account can cost us in a calendar month, and is that number enforced in code or written in a policy? Caught late, the ceiling gets installed during an incident and lands on legitimate users.

Farming and abuse. The early warning is falling median time from signup to first action at scale, and a rising share of disposable email domains. The diagnostic: if I wanted to resell our free tier, how would I do it, and what would stop me? Caught late, the response is indistinguishable from a service degradation.

Shadow free usage inside paying accounts. The early warning is free accounts registered on the email domains of existing customers, growing faster than paid seats at those customers. The diagnostic: how many of our top fifty accounts have more free users than paid users? Caught late, you meet it across the table at renewal, where the customer has already proved to themselves that they can live on the free tier.

The unretractable promise. The early warning is the phrase "free forever" in marketing copy with no accompanying grandfathering policy. The diagnostic: write today the memo you would send if we had to halve the free tier — who receives it, and what do they do? Caught late, you get Chinar's eleven days.

No owner. The early warning is that the free tier appears in no single recurring review. The diagnostic: who is accountable for free-tier gross margin, and what is their budget for this year? If the answer takes more than five seconds, the free tier is expanding by accretion. Caught late, the correction arrives from finance as a cut rather than from product as a design.

Anchoring the category at zero. The early warning is competitors matching within two quarters and sales calls that now open with "why isn't this free?" The diagnostic: if every competitor matched this within ninety days, would we still do it? Caught late, there is no individual remedy at all; the category's reference price has moved and no single firm can move it back.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does freemium lower customer acquisition cost, or relabel it? The distribution school points to products whose blended CAC fell by an order of magnitude after a free tier launched, and argues that free-tier cost of goods sold is simply a more efficient form of marketing spend, with the added advantage that it produces a durable asset. The accounting sceptics reply that this is selection, not causation: free tiers are adopted disproportionately by products that were already spreading, so the observed CAC collapse is confounded, and moving marketing spend into cost of goods sold flatters gross-margin-adjusted CAC in ways that do not survive a careful recomputation. The sceptics have the better of the methodology; the distribution school has the better of the existence proofs. What would settle it is a well-powered randomised geography holdout with ACV measured against a matched control — exactly what Chitralekha ran, at small scale, and which gave the sceptics the win in that instance. Very few such experiments exist, and almost none are published.

Should AI-native products have free tiers at all? One camp argues the cost curve resolves this: the price of a given capability has fallen by more than an order of magnitude in short periods, so a free tier that is marginal today is comfortable in eighteen months, and the installed base you build meanwhile is not recoverable later. The opposing camp argues that per-user consumption is growing faster than per-unit cost is falling — longer contexts, multi-step reasoning, agentic loops that make dozens of calls where one used to suffice — so that the fully loaded cost per free account is rising in practice even as unit prices fall. A third position holds that the free tier is correctly run at a loss because it is the cheapest available source of evaluation data and real-world distribution shift, which is a genuine asset in a way that free users of conventional software never were; its opponents reply that data-protection consent regimes make that asset far less usable than its advocates assume. All three positions are held by serious people and the evidence is two or three years from being decisive.

Is the reverse trial the best of both, or the worst of both? Giving every new user full access for a fixed period and then dropping them to a permanent free tier restores the trial's forcing event while keeping the free tier's reservoir. Its advocates point to conversion hazards that stay elevated well past the drop-down, as Chitralekha's second cohort did. Its critics make a more subtle argument: the reverse trial deliberately creates an experience of loss, and users who have had a capability removed evaluate the paid product against what they had rather than against what they need, which can suppress willingness to pay for years and generates measurable ill-will. This is the liveliest current disagreement in packaging practice, and there is no clean evidence either way, partly because the companies that run reverse trials do not publish the cohorts that did not convert.

Can a free tier ever be sunset? The never-retract camp treats free tiers as irreversible and argues that the only safe policy is to launch conservatively and loosen. The retract-early camp points at the companies that did tighten and survived — the withdrawal of free dynos, the end of unlimited free photo storage, repeated tightening at note-taking and design products — and argues that the backlash is loud, short and confined to a population that was never going to pay, while the margin improvement is permanent. Both are describing real cases. What separates them, in the author's reading, is whether the free tier had become infrastructure for someone else's product: where third parties built on the free tier, retraction is catastrophic; where they did not, it is merely unpleasant.

Do free-to-paid conversion benchmarks mean anything? The familiar "two to five percent" figure circulates as though it were a constant. Its defenders argue it is a useful prior and that deviation from it is informative. Its critics point out that the denominator is undefined: registered accounts, monthly actives, activated accounts and accounts that reached a specific value event give conversion rates that differ by a factor of twenty for the same business, and that firms choose the denominator that flatters. The critics are, on the merits, straightforwardly right. The benchmark survives because boards ask for it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can recite the distinction between freemium and a trial, name the three gating mechanisms, and warn about cost to serve. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in five observable ways.

They ask for different data. Before the conversion rate, they want the hazard by tenure; before the mean cost, the ninety-ninth percentile; before the signup lift, a matched-control measurement of what happened to ACV. They are comfortable saying that a proposal cannot be evaluated yet because the hazard curve does not exist.

They name the school they are arguing from. In a disagreement about a free tier, they will say out loud "I am making a distribution argument and you are making a carrying-cost argument, and those are not in conflict; here is the number that decides between them." This single habit shortens most pricing arguments by weeks.

They treat the free tier's design as a sorting problem rather than a generosity problem. The question is never "what can we afford to give away" but "what can we give away that the buyer with money still cannot use". They can state, in one sentence, what their free tier denies an enterprise, and they can state that the denial has nothing to do with the vendor's costs.

They write the exit before the entrance. The grandfathering policy, the change-of-terms language, the kill criterion with a number attached and a named owner — all of it exists before launch, not because they expect to use it, but because writing it forces the question of whether the commitment is one the company can actually keep. Chitralekha's pilot was labelled a pilot inside the product, with an end date visible to users, which is why it could be ended without a single complaint.

And they are willing to let cost to serve be someone else's problem to solve. The mark of a genuinely senior practitioner in this area is that they spend at least as much time with the infrastructure team as with the pricing consultant, because they know that halving the cost of a free user is often cheaper, faster and less damaging than halving what the free user gets.

12. What each of them decided

Ravindran brought three recommendations to Chitralekha's board on 28 November 2025, and the board accepted all three. First, the free tier would ship, but on an inverted gate: one editor, no audit trail, no system-of-record integration, no programmatic access — buyer-shaped rather than cost-shaped — with a monthly document ceiling set generously at the ninety-fifth percentile of observed human usage and enforced absolutely in code. Second, every new account would begin with a fourteen-day reverse trial at full capability, to restore the forcing event that the pilot's first cohort had lacked; Ravindran recorded her own reservation in the minutes, noting the loss-aversion objection and committing to measure it. Third, the enterprise segment — accounts above 500 employees, where deal data showed the free tier was doing no qualification work at all — would continue to be sold through a sales-assisted trial, and free signups from those domains would be routed to a human within a day.

The projected arithmetic, which Salunke signed: signups of 1,280 a month, a conversion hazard of 0.9%, a dormancy hazard of 11%, a steady-state free base of about 10,756 accounts costing ₹1.29 crore a year, and roughly 97 new paying accounts a month against the trial's 37. The required signup multiplier fell from 5.34× to 1.18× against an observed 3.1×. Salunke's written caveat, which deserves as much weight as the model, was that the 0.9% hazard came from a self-selected cohort of 1,180 accounts over six months and might not survive contact with the full funnel; the board agreed to a review at month nine with an explicit reversion path, available because the free tier was being launched with a change-of-terms clause and a published grandfathering rule from day one.

At Chandrabhaga, Pathak and Bhagat took a package to the board on 19 December 2025. The promise on the box would be honoured exactly as written for every device already sold — no reduction in retention, resolution or features for the installed base, ever. For devices sold from 1 April 2026, the box would carry a different line: telemetry and the standard app included for sixty months, renewable thereafter at a published ₹240 a year per device. The new paid tier, Chandrabhaga Insight at ₹900 per site per month, would gate on multi-site rollup, statutory energy-audit report formats, ISO 50001 export and application programming interface access — things a single shop floor never asks for and a group with eleven plants cannot operate without. And engineering would ship adaptive sampling in the first quarter, storing one-second resolution only in windows around detected events, which modelling suggested would cut mean cost per device from ₹96 to ₹41 without any customer noticing a difference.

The board's discussion spent almost no time on Insight's price and almost all of it on the sixty-month line on the box. Bhagat's argument carried: the alternative was not a longer promise but a promise the company would eventually break. Distributor testing in Rajkot and Surat had already shown what she expected — buyers of capital equipment read a sixty-month inclusion and a published renewal price as a normal annual maintenance contract, and it moved hardware conversion by nothing measurable.

Three questions for discussion.

1. Chitralekha's decision turned on raising the conversion hazard from 0.22% to 0.9% by changing the gating axis. Suppose the month-nine review shows the full-funnel hazard settling at 0.45% instead. The required signup multiplier becomes roughly 2.2× against an observed 3.1× — still a pass, but with much less room. At what hazard should Ravindran reverse, and what exactly would she do on the day she decided to, given that 40,000 accounts would by then be on the free tier?

2. Chinar Collab's price compression — a 23% fall in new-business ACV — was larger in rupee terms than its cannibalisation and far larger than its cloud bill, yet it was the last of the three effects the company measured. What would have to be true of a company's instrumentation, and of its organisational structure, for the price effect of a free tier to be measured before launch rather than eighteen months after?

3. Chandrabhaga chose to honour a promise made in 2017 that it now knows was mispriced, at a cost of roughly ₹1.6 crore a year against 14,200 ageing devices. Was that the right call, or is it a sentimental decision dressed as an ethical one? What would change your answer: the size of the installed base, the identity of the customers, or whether a competitor was about to make the same promise?

13. Going deeper

  1. Packaging: good / better / best — the free tier is the zeroth rung of a ladder, and it cannot be designed sensibly in isolation from the rungs above it. This topic supplies the discipline of building a coherent tier structure, which is what turns θL and θH from a two-point model into an actual price list.
  2. Case: Dropbox — the canonical worked example of a free tier designed around a value metric (storage) that was simultaneously the cost driver, the sharing mechanism and the referral currency. It is the clearest illustration of the rare case where cost-shaped gating is also buyer-shaped, and worth studying precisely because that alignment is so hard to reproduce.
  3. AI cost-to-serve and pricing — the direct sequel to sections 3 and 5 here. If the marginal cost of a unit of value is no longer near zero, the entire architecture of software pricing built since 2006 requires re-derivation, and this topic works through what survives and what does not.
  4. When to charge — the question this page answers for the free tier, asked across the whole customer lifetime: at what moment in a relationship is the ask made, and what does the timing itself signal. Free-tier design is a special case of it.
  5. Willingness-to-pay research — the discipline that supplies vH and vL. Nothing in section 3 can be computed without it, and the single most common reason teams argue in circles about free tiers is that they have never measured either quantity.
  6. The value metric — what you count and charge for. The free tier's limits are expressed in the value metric, so a badly chosen metric makes a well-designed free tier impossible; Chinar's inversion from boards to editors was a value-metric change disguised as a packaging change.
  7. What pricing signals — a price of zero is the loudest signal in the catalogue, and it is read differently by an individual user, a procurement committee and a competitor. This topic supplies the vocabulary for the anchoring and commitment arguments in sections 4 and 9.
  8. Value-based, cost-plus and competitive pricing — the three pricing logics, and the reason the carrying-cost school and the distribution school talk past each other: they are, at bottom, cost-plus and value-based reasoning applied to the same artefact.
  9. Discounting and promotions — the nearest relative of the free tier and its most frequent substitute. Much of what a free tier does can be achieved by a time-bounded discount with none of the ratchet, and knowing when to reach for which is a large part of packaging judgement.
